edition.locus: Against Marcion 1.13 (world not unworthy of God the Creator)

source_text: Cum deum hoc gradu expellimus, cui nulla conditio\' tam propria et deo digna quam creatoris testimonium praesignarit, narem contrahentes impudentissimi Marcionitae conuertuntur ad destructionem operum creatoris. \'nimirum\', inquiunt. \'grande opus et dignum deo mundus\'! numquid ergo ereator minime deus? plane deus. ergo nec mundus deo indignus: nihil etenim deus indignum se fecisset, etsi mundum homini.\' non sibi fecit, etsi omne opus inferius est suo artifice. et tamen, si quale quid fecisse indignum est deo, quanto indignius deo est nihil eum omnino fecisse! ** uel indignum, quo posset etiam digniorum auctor sperari. ut ergo aliquid + et de isto huius mundi indigno loquar, cui et apud Graecos ornamenti et cultus, non sordium, nomen est, indignas uidelicet substantias ipsi illi sapientiae professores, de quorum ingeniis omnis haeresis animatur. deos pronuntiauerunt, ut Thales aquam, ut Heraclitus ignem, ut Anaximenes aerem. ut Anaximander uniuersa caelestia, ut Strato caelum et terram, ut Zeno aerem et aetherem, ut Plato sidera, quae genus deorum igneum appellat, cum de mundo, considerando scilicet et magnitudinem et uim et potestatem et honorem et decorem, opem fidem legem singulorum elementorum, quae omnibus gignendis alendis conficiendis reficiendisque conspirant, ut plerique physicorum, formidauerint, [initium ac finem mundo constare] ne substantiae eius, tantae scilicet, minus dei haberentur, quas colunt et Persarum magi et Aegyptiorum hierophantae et Indorum gymnosophistae. ipsa quoque uulgaris superstitio communis idolatriae, cum in simulacris de nominibus et fabulis ueterum mortuorum pudet, ad interpretationem naturalium refugit et dedecus suum ingenio obumbrat, figurans Iouem in substantiam feruidam et Iunonem eius in aeream secundum sonum Graecorum uocabulorum. item Vestam in ignem et Camenas in aquam et Magnam Matrem in terram seminalia demessam, lacertis aratam, lauacris rigatam. sic et, Osiris quod semper sepelitur et in uiuido quaeritur et cum gaudio inuenitur, reciprocarum frugum et uiuidorum elementorum et recidiui anni fidem argumentantur, sicut aridae et ardentis naturae sacramenta leones Mithrae philosophantur. et superiores quidem situ aut statu substantias sufficit facilius deos habitas quam deo indignas. ad humilia deficiam? unus, opinor, de sepibus flosculus, non dico de pratis, una cuiuslibet maris conchula, non dico de rubro, una tetraonis pinnula, taceo de pauo, sordidum artificem pronuntiabit tibi creatorem?
pass_a_gloss: Mundus non indignus Deo. Philosophi elementa deos; flos/concha artificem probant.
pass_b_english: When we drive God out from this rank, for whom no condition so proper and worthy of God has pre-signed testimony as of Creator, the most shameless Marcionites, contracting the nose, turn to destruction of the Creator’s works. ‘Doubtless,’ they say, ‘a grand work and worthy of God is the world!’ Is the Creator therefore least God? Clearly God. Therefore neither is the world unworthy of God: for God would have made nothing unworthy of himself, even if he made the world for the human, not for himself, even if every work is lower than its artisan. And yet, if it is unworthy of God to have made such a thing, how much more unworthy of God is it that he have made nothing at all!—or something unworthy, by which he could even be hoped author of worthier things.

So then to say something also about this ‘unworthy’ of this world, which even among the Greeks has the name of ornament and culture, not of filth—those very professors of wisdom, from whose talents every heresy is animated, have pronounced as gods the ‘unworthy’ substances: as Thales water, as Heraclitus fire, as Anaximenes air, as Anaximander all the celestials, as Strato heaven and earth, as Zeno air and ether, as Plato the stars, which he calls a fiery genus of gods—when about the world, considering of course both the greatness and force and power and honor and beauty, the help, faith, law of the several elements which conspire for generating, nourishing, completing, and repairing all things, as most of the physicists have feared lest its substances, so great of course, be held less than gods—which the Magi of the Persians and the hierophants of the Egyptians and the gymnosophists of the Indians also worship.

Common superstition of ordinary idolatry too, when it is ashamed in images from the names and tales of old dead men, flees to an interpretation of natural things and shadows its disgrace with ingenuity, figuring Jupiter into a fiery substance and his Juno into an airy one according to the sound of Greek words; likewise Vesta into fire and the Camenae into water and the Great Mother into earth—harvested of seeds, plowed with arms, watered with washings. So also that Osiris is always buried and sought in the living and found with joy they argue as the faith of reciprocating fruits and living elements and the returning year, just as they philosophize the lions of Mithras as sacraments of dry and burning nature. And for substances higher by site or status it is enough that they have been more easily held gods than unworthy of God. Shall I sink to low things? One little flower from hedges, I do not say from meadows; one little shell of any sea, I do not say from the Red; one little wing-feather of a francolin—I am silent about the peacock—will pronounce the Creator a sordid artisan for you?
